rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite the pagans' refusal to worship God alone, angels and earthly believers prostrate willingly, while unbelievers do so unwillingly when compelled.
rows.anchor: ولله يسجد من في السموات والأرض طوعا وكرها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says believers prostrate willingly, whereas unbelievers prostrate unwillingly.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: {ولله يسجد من في السموات والأرض طوعا وكرها}

rows.speaker: ربيع بن خثيم
rows.claim: When reciting the verse, Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym responds, “Indeed, my Lord,” affirming it reverently.
rows.anchor: إذا تلا هذه الآية: {ولله يسجد من في السموات والأرض طوعا وكرها} قال: «بلى يا رباه»

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explains willing submission as entering Islam voluntarily and unwilling submission as entering only under the sword.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد في قوله: {ولله يسجد من في السموات والأرض طوعا وكرها}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shadows of all who prostrate to God also prostrate morning and evening, as each person's shadow shifts in the evening; compare 16:48.
rows.anchor: ولله يسجد من في السموات والأرض طوعا وكرها وظلالهم بالغدو والآصال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses the phrase as the time when someone's shadow falls to his right or left.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قوله: {وظلالهم بالغدو والآصال} [الرعد: 15]

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: In the interpretation of Mujahid, a believer's shadow prostrates willingly while a disbeliever's shadow does so willingly although he himself is reluctant.
rows.anchor: قال في تفسير مجاهد: {ولله يسجد من في السموات والأرض طوعا وكرها وظلالهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the shadows of all things prostrate to God, citing the shadows that prostrate while humbled.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد في قوله: {وظلالهم بالغدو والآصال} [الرعد: 15]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-āṣāl is the plural of aṣl, itself the plural of aṣīl, meaning evening from afternoon until sunset; Abu Dhuʾayb's verse uses al-aṣāʾil in this sense.
rows.anchor: والآصال: جمع أصل، والأصل: جمع أصيل، والأصيل: هو العشي، وهو ما بين العصر إلى مغرب الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two parables compare truth and falsehood, and faith and disbelief: truth remains beneficial while falsehood vanishes.
rows.anchor: وهذا مثل ضربه الله للحق والباطل، والإيمان به والكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The valleys carry water according to their capacities, the larger carrying more and the smaller less; the water represents truth and its rising foam falsehood.
rows.anchor: ذلك الماء الذي أنزله الله من السماء زبدا عاليا فوق السيل

words: وَمِمَّا يُوقِدُونَ عَلَيْهِ فِى ٱلنَّارِ ٱبْتِغَآءَ حِلْيَةٍ أَوْ مَتَٰعٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parable is metal fired to obtain gold or silver ornaments and useful goods such as copper, lead, and iron; dross is falsehood and the useful pure metal remains.
rows.anchor: ومثل آخر للحق والباطل، مثل فضة أو ذهب يوقد عليها الناس في النار طلب حلية يتخذونها أو متاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foam on floodwater and the dross of fired metals are carried off by wind or water, thrown against trees and valley sides, and become useless.
rows.anchor: فيذهب بدفع الرياح وقذف الماء به وتعلقه بالأشجار وجوانب الوادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun al-zabad is nominative under the construction “and among what they fire in the furnace is foam,” with the implied comparison to flood foam.
rows.anchor: ورفع {الزبد} [الرعد: 17] بقوله: {ومما يوقدون عليه في النار}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas compares hearts receiving the parable to valleys receiving water according to their certainty or doubt: doubt does not benefit, while certainty does; foam is doubt and lasting water is certainty.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قوله: {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the flood carries wood and manure, while useful water and purified metals illustrate good deeds, guidance, and truth that endure; on Judgment Day falsehood disappears and the people of truth benefit.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قوله: {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها فاحتمل السيل زبدا رابيا} [الرعد: 17]

words: وَمِمَّا يُوقِدُونَ عَلَيْهِ فِى ٱلنَّارِ ٱبْتِغَآءَ حِلْيَةٍ أَوْ مَتَٰعٍۢ
rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains ornaments as gold and silver and useful goods as copper and iron; firing removes impurity, just as truth remains for its adherents to benefit from.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن، في قوله: {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية} [الرعد: 17] إلى: {أو متاع زبد مثله} [الرعد: 17]

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says each valley holds as much as it can; metal goods include iron, copper, and lead, whose dross resembles flood foam, and the water and foam represent truth and falsehood.
rows.anchor: أنه سمع مجاهدا، يقول: " {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17] قال: ما أطاقت ملأها

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj glosses the foam's going as its freezing on the ground, and says the water that remains is the beneficial element; both images represent truth and falsehood.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج: قوله: " {فأما الزبد فيذهب جفاء} [الرعد: 17] قال: جمودا في الأرض

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says each valley carries water according to its size and the foam rises high; he describes three examples in one parable, with vanishing foam as falsehood and enduring water and refined metal as truth.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: " {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17] الصغير بصغره

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains al-jufāʾ as matter that clings to trees; the foam becomes useless and loses any hoped-for blessing, like falsehood.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: " {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17]

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies useful goods as iron and ṣufr (copper/brass); after its dross is removed, the useful metal remains, just as truth remains for its people.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: " {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17]

rows.speaker: عوف
rows.claim: A report reaching ʿAwf says valleys carry water by their size; foam is scattered by wind, while pure water remains for drink, crops, and use, and useful purified metal remains as well.
rows.anchor: قال: ثنا عوف، قال: بلغني في قوله: {أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17]

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd applies the parable to truth and falsehood: foam and dross are useless, while water and sound jewelry remain and benefit people.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد في قوله: {ومما يوقدون عليه في النار ابتغاء حلية أو متاع زبد مثله} [الرعد: 17]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the small valley carries according to its small size and the large valley according to its large size.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: {أودية بقدرها} [الرعد: 17] قال: «الصغير بصغره، والكبير بكبره»

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says truth is like the floodwater that stays in the earth, while falsehood is like foam that does not benefit people.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء، «ضرب الله مثلا للحق والباطل فضرب مثل الحق كمثل السيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rābiyan means high or swollen, from rabā/yurbi; rābiya also names a raised mound, and 22:5 uses the same root for the earth swelling.
rows.anchor: من قولهم: ربا الشيء يربو ربوا فهو راب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The metals are called matāʿ because people make use of them; matāʿ broadly means anything people enjoy, as the poet's line about what remains before death illustrates.
rows.anchor: وقيل للنحاس والرصاص والحديد في هذا الموضع: المتاع، لأنه يستمتع به، وكل ما يتمتع به الناس فهو متاع

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlā says a pot “jafaʾa” when, as it boils, its foam pours out, or when it settles and no foam remains.
rows.anchor: عن أبي عبيدة معمر بن المثنى قال: قال أبو عمرو بن العلاء: يقال: قد أجفأت القدر، وذلك إذا غلت فانصب زبدها

rows.speaker: بعض أهل العربية من أهل البصرة
rows.claim: Some Basran grammarians say the foam is absorbed by the earth; they connect jafā and ajfā to drying, while injafā describes a valley bringing down flood debris.
rows.anchor: زعم بعض أهل العربية من أهل البصرة أن معنى قوله: {فيذهب جفاء} [الرعد: 17] تنشفه الأرض

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Arabic usage says jafaʾtu the pot means to pour out its foam, ajfaʾtuhu is another form, and jafaʾtu a man means to knock him down.
rows.anchor: وذكر عن العرب أنها تقول: جفأت القدر أجفؤها: إذا أخرجت جفاءها، وهو الزبد الذي يعلوها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One analysis treats jufāʾ as jufʾan, a verbal noun used as a noun; Arabic similarly uses forms such as qumāsh, duqāq, huṭām, and ghuthāʾ as nouns.
rows.anchor: وقيل: {فيذهب جفاء} [الرعد: 17] بمعنى جفئا، لأنه مصدر من قول القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cry was a thunderbolt of punishment that struck them as the sun rose; “they were cried out against” means they were destroyed.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج: {فأخذتهم الصيحة مشرقين} [الحجر: 73]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mushriqīn and muṣbiḥīn are accusative circumstantial expressions meaning that they were at sunrise or morning.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج: {فأخذتهم الصيحة مشرقين} [الحجر: 73]

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says they were struck when the sun had risen, which is what “at sunrise” means.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج: {فأخذتهم الصيحة مشرقين} [الحجر: 73]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God develops a human from a lowly drop through successive stages in three darknesses, breathes in the spirit, and feeds and grows him to maturity; the human then denies the creator and disputes with Him.
rows.anchor: ونفخ فيه الروح، فغذاه ورزقه القوت ونماه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human forgets the one who formed him and argues against God, even asking who can revive decayed bones, as in 36:78.
rows.anchor: فقال {من يحيي العظام وهي رميم} [يس: 78]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubīn means that a person makes his dispute clear through articulate speech and argument with his tongue.
rows.anchor: ويعني بالمبين: أنه يبين عن خصومته بمنطقه ويجادل بلسانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-insān is grammatically singular here but denotes humanity as a whole.
rows.anchor: وعنى بالإنسان: جميع الناس، أخرج بلفظ الواحد وهو في معنى الجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rawāsī is the plural of rāsiyah and means the firm mountains fixed in the earth.
rows.anchor: وألقى في الأرض رواسي أن تميد بكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause means “lest the earth sway with you,” with “not” understood, as in 4:176 where God makes matters clear so that people do not go astray.
rows.anchor: وألقى في الأرض رواسي أن تميد بكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God anchored the earth with mountains to stop its inhabitants from being shaken; it had been moving before the mountains were set in place.
rows.anchor: أرسى الأرض بالجبال لئلا يميد خلقه الذي على ظهرها، بل وقد كانت مائدة قبل أن ترسى بها

rows.speaker: قيس بن عباد
rows.claim: A report from Qays ibn ʿAbbād says the newly created earth churned and the angels feared it could not bear anyone; by morning its mountains had appeared.
rows.anchor: عن قيس بن عباد: " أن الله تبارك وتعالى لما خلق الأرض جعلت تمور

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that the earth heaved and protested that people would sin and make it foul; God anchored it with visible and unseen mountains, leaving it stable like quivering flesh.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن أبي طالب، قال: " لما خلق الله الأرض قمصت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mayd means unsteady movement or rocking; a ship may roll and tilt with its passengers, and the word also names sea sickness or vertigo.
rows.anchor: والميد: هو الاضطراب والتكفؤ، يقال: مادت السفينة تميد ميدا: إذا تكفأت بأهلها ومالت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses the clause as meaning that the earth might tilt with you.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد: " {أن تميد بكم} [النحل: 15] أن تكفأ بكم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the mountains keep the earth from swaying; he also says it nearly moved at creation, then mountains appeared, whose origin the angels did not know.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، عن الحسن، في قوله: {وألقى في الأرض رواسي أن تميد بكم} [النحل: 15]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And rivers” is coordinated with the mountains and shares the implied verb “He placed/made”; the intended meaning is clear despite the verb not being repeated, as in the cited rajaz line where a non-heard quality is coordinated with sound.
rows.anchor: فعطف بالأنهار على الرواسي، وأعمل فيها ما أعمل في الرواسي، إذ كان مفهوما معنى الكلام والمراد منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subul is the plural of sabīl, like ṭuruq is the plural of ṭarīq; the paths and passes let people travel for their needs and livelihoods, as a mercy and blessing.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: " {سبلا} [طه: 53] أي طرقا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses subul as roads or routes, citing the same word in 20:53.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: " {سبلا} [طه: 53] أي طرقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paths allow people to find their intended places and destinations without getting lost or confused.
rows.anchor: لكي تهتدوا بهذه السبل التي جعلها لكم في الأرض إلى الأماكن التي تقصدون، والمواضع التي تريدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent a messenger to every past nation, as He did to the present audience, commanding worship of God alone, exclusive obedience, and sincere devotion.
rows.anchor: فيكم بأن اعبدوا الله وحده لا شريك له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ṭāghūt to avoid refers here to Satan, whose misguidance and diversion from God's path people must fear.
rows.anchor: يقول: وابعدوا من الشيطان، واحذروا أن يغويكم ويصدكم عن سبيل الله

words: فَمِنْهُم مَّنْ هَدَى ٱللَّهُ وَمِنْهُم مَّنْ حَقَّتْ عَلَيْهِ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some nations were guided to believe the messengers and obey God, so they prospered and escaped punishment; others disbelieved, denied messengers, followed ṭāghūt, and God destroyed them.
rows.anchor: فممن بعثنا فيهم رسلنا من هدى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After birth, God teaches people what they did not know and gives them reason to understand and distinguish good from evil; He enables them to see and hear after they had known nothing.
rows.anchor: والله أخرجكم من بطون أمهاتكم لا تعلمون شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing receives sounds and lets people understand one another's conversation; sight sees people, allowing recognition and distinction between them.
rows.anchor: السمع الذي تسمعون به الأصوات، فيفقه بعضكم عن بعض ما تتحاورون به بينكم، والأبصار التي تبصرون بها الأشخاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afʾidah are hearts by which people know and retain things, reflect on them, and understand them.
rows.anchor: يقول: والقلوب التي تعرفون بها الأشياء فتحفظونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God bestowed these faculties so people would thank Him alone, not idols or partners that had no share in His blessings; the phrase is cited also at 2:52.
rows.anchor: فعلنا ذلك بكم، فاشكروا الله على ما أنعم به عليكم من ذلك، دون الآلهة والأنداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The birth clause is a complete statement, followed by a new clause about the faculties; physical faculties were given before birth, but knowledge and reason after birth.
rows.anchor: كلام متناه، ثم ابتدئ الخبر، فقيل: وجعل الله لكم السمع والأبصار والأفئدة وإنما قلنا ذلك كذلك
